title: How closely did Canada’s high-oil scenario track inflation? The evidence behind Gravelle’s speech
summary: In Edmonton, Deputy Governor Toni Gravelle offered a way to read a central-bank scenario as a testable conditional forecast. In April, oil was around US$100 per barrel. The Bank’s base case assumed a decline toward US$75 by mid-2027 and a return of inflation to 2% in early 2027. Its alternative assumed that oil stayed expensive, keeping inflation near 3% for more than a year and calling for consecutive rate increases. By October, oil was still around US$100, refinery margins were elevated and domestic activity had been stronger than the Bank expected. Inflation had tracked the alternative more closely. Gravelle explained why this affected the Bank’s assessment without claiming that all assumptions in the alternative had materialized.

The chart data allow the claim to be checked. For 2026 Q2, the April inflation baseline was 2.6%, its high-oil alternative was 2.9%, and the corresponding value in the October series was 3.0%. For Q3 the three figures were 2.2%, 2.8% and 3.0%. Using the October-vintage values as the reference for those two completed quarters, the April baseline missed by an average of 0.60 percentage points in absolute terms. The alternative missed by 0.15 points. That difference of 0.45 points measures closeness across two observations. It says nothing by itself about what probability the Bank had attached to the alternative in April or how much of the inflation surprise was caused by oil.

The comparison changes for 2026 Q4. April’s baseline had inflation at 2.2%, its alternative at 3.0%, and the October baseline at 3.4%. For 2027 Q1 the respective figures were 2.0%, 3.1% and 3.5%. Both quarters were in the future when Gravelle spoke. By then the Bank expected inflation to exceed even the earlier high-oil path for a time. Stronger activity, elevated refinery margins and changes in trade conditions also shaped its assessment. Comparing these vintages cannot isolate the effect of oil alone.

Gravelle’s historical examples show why accuracy against a later outcome is sometimes the wrong test. Early in the pandemic the Bank could not identify a most likely path for output. Chart 1 shows a range of real GDP levels for 2020 Q2. Relative to the preceding quarter on each scenario’s own line, the lower path fell from 2,034 to 1,467, around 28%, and the upper path from 2,079 to 1,786, around 14%. These are changes in quarterly GDP levels in chained 2012 dollars. The Bank assigned no probability to either endpoint.

The July 2022 example asked how much more costly disinflation could become if firms and workers began to expect continuing price increases. Faster wage and price adjustment would require tighter policy and would depress output. Chart 2 puts 2023 Q1 real GDP growth at an annualized −1.74% in that scenario and +1.65% in the base case. The difference is 3.39 percentage points of annualized quarterly growth. The wage-price spiral never materialized. Its purpose was to show a risk to the economy and to explain why the Bank had raised its rate forcefully.

Publishing scenarios can help investors understand how the Bank would react as conditions change. Gravelle identified a cost to publishing a precise rate path. If investors relied on that path and did less independent analysis, market prices would reveal less about their assessment of the economy. He distinguished emergency guidance at the effective lower bound from routine guidance. The consecutive rate increases in the high-oil scenario illustrate a response conditional on a particular shock. Gravelle announced no November rate decision. The Bank also selects among the many scenarios it studies. Publishing an alternative makes sense when uncertainty is extreme or when a material risk is hard to explain in words alone.

questions.question: How much better did the oil alternative perform, and what would count as an honest out-of-sample test?
questions.detail: Freeze the April assumptions, retain the same year-over-year quarterly CPI measure and use first releases as each quarter arrives. The speech’s two-quarter comparison uses October-vintage values. Were similar conclusions possible in real time? Treat the Q4 2026 and later October numbers as forecasts, and track whether the conditioning oil path was actually met.

questions.question: Did investors learn about the Bank’s response to oil or just receive a new oil-price assumption?
questions.detail: Separate news about oil futures, refinery margins and Canadian activity from news about the Bank’s response. Compare rate pricing around the April publication, the October decision and the November speech. Each occasion gave investors a different information set. International announcements during a long event window could easily obscure the effect.

questions.question: How should a communication score handle a simulated series of hikes?
questions.detail: Identify the speaker, the conditioning assumption and the date of any actual decision. The series of increases appears in April’s hypothetical high-oil case. The October decision and this retrospective account are different observations. Would coding every tightening verb as a new rate signal double-count information?

questions.question: Can a scenario be informative even when it never occurs?
questions.detail: Use the problem the Bank was trying to solve. The pandemic exercise supplied bounds without probability weights. The wage-price scenario described a costly change in behaviour. The oil alternative gave observable conditions against which later evidence could be tested. For each, what could a household or investor infer about how a change in conditions would affect policy?
